title: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
hookLine: have We not given him two eyes, a tongue and lips, and shown him two ways (90:8–10)
tomorrow: Al-Fajr: the dawn and ten nights

cards: Try this. Touch your eyelids, gently. Then your lips.

Then press your tongue against the back of your teeth. All three have been busy all day, mostly without a thought: reading this screen, talking to the barista, tasting the coffee, muttering at the traffic.

Equipment doesn't get more ordinary than this. Right before the steep path, Al-Balad stops and points at exactly this equipment, and asks a question about it. Then it adds one more gift that you can't touch at all.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO THINKS NO ONE SEES.
teach.b: Al-Balad describes a man who boasts that he has spent heaps of money and thinks no one sees him.

teach.h: EYES, TONGUE, AND LIPS THAT CLOSE.
teach.b: The surah answers with a question, verse eight, in Pickthall's words: Did We not assign unto him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips? The man who thinks no one sees him was given the power to see.
The man bragging with his mouth was given the mouth. It's a gentle, almost funny reversal: everything he's using to show off was handed to him. Why two lips, and not just a mouth?

Some commentators notice that lips close. The tongue can speak, and the lips can hold it back; the same equipment can say the cruel thing or keep it in. Then verse ten: and We showed him the two ways.
The Arabic is an-najdayn, the two raised roads, the two highland paths.

teach.h: GIVEN THE TOOLS, SHOWN THE ROADS.
teach.b: Ibn Kathir gives the common reading: the way of good and the way of harm, both shown clearly, like two roads on a ridge you can see from far off.
He also reports a few who read it more tenderly, as the two sources of milk a newborn is guided to without being taught. Either way, guidance was given before you asked for it.
Eyes to see the roads, a tongue to speak on the good one, lips to stop at the other. Then verse eleven, from yesterday: but he did not attempt the steep path.
So the surah's logic runs: you were given the tools, you were shown the roads, now climb.

how: Muslims often recall these verses of Al-Balad when speaking of guarding the tongue, a theme that runs through many hadith, and of gratitude for the senses as gifts that come with responsibility.

o: a village of herders out in the desert
the city, Surah ninety of the Qur'an
a mountain far from any town

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: given to the one who thinks no one sees
they can close on the tongue

s: Al-Balad asks about eyes, tongue and lips to answer a boaster
the man who thinks no one sees him was given eyes; the one bragging was given a mouth.
every commentator reads the two ways as good and evil
it's the common reading, but Ibn Kathir also reports a few who read it as a newborn guided to milk.
the surah says people are left to find the roads alone
it says We showed him the two ways: guidance came first.

games.q: a man boasts of the fortune he's spent and thinks nobody sees him. how does Al-Balad answer?
o: by asking: did We not give him two eyes?
by telling him to spend more
games.why: a question, not a lecture: the eyes, tongue and lips he's using were given to him, and so were the two roads.

practice: Rest your attention on your mouth: the tongue resting, the lips closed. Then think of one thing you could say that would help someone, a thank you, an apology, a word of praise to someone who never hears it.
Keep the lips closed for now, and just choose the words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Balad. The city, Surah ninety: eyes, a tongue, two lips, and the two roads shown. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "the two raised roads," the dual of najd, high ground (Qur'an 90:10).

carryVoice: Your line: two roads shown. The same tongue can take either one. See you at dawn.
